title: Which principle is being applied?
blurb: Identify which of the seven PRINCE2 principles an agile action applies, and separate the near-miss principles by their reason.
question: Saltmarsh's board sets zero time and cost tolerance but lets the number of features in each release vary. Which principle is being applied, and why?

teach.h: Seven principles, applied the agile way
teach.body: Formally: the seven PRINCE2 principles are ensure continued business justification, learn from experience, define roles, responsibilities and relationships, manage by stages, manage by exception, focus on products, and tailor to suit the project. The principles themselves are not tailored; how they are applied is. In plain English: in an agile scenario, ask what the action is FOR, then match that purpose to a principle and check the reason fits.

teach.h: Each principle in an agile project
head: Principle
Agile application
Stem cue
rows: Flex what is delivered, fix time and cost

teach.caption: Other branches: who does what (roles); authorizing one stage at a time (stages); fitting the method to the context (tailor).

rows.label: Core idea
values: Plan and authorize stage by stage

teach.h: Manage by exception: the heart of self-management
teach.body: Management by exception sets tolerances for the seven performance aspects and delegates within them. In agile it is at the heart of empowering people to self-manage while staying in control: allow tolerance on what is delivered, restrict tolerance on time and cost. Varying levels of agile maturity are not escalated as exceptions; they are handled openly as lessons are learned.

teach.caption: The board authorizes one stage at a time; each stage holds a release made of iterations.

items: Find the action: what did the board, PM or team actually do?
Ask its purpose: value, learning, roles, stage control, tolerances, outputs or fit to context.
Check the reason in the option: it must explain THIS action, not just be true.
Watch role detail: the CPO, not the project manager, makes sure user requirements are met.

teach.body: At Saltmarsh Housing Group, the board fixes the £1.3 million budget and twelve months but lets the number of features flex (manage by exception). The chief executive sets a measurable fall in second visits as the minimum worth having (continued business justification). The service design team runs retrospectives each iteration (learn from experience). If project manager Sally Greaves records in the PID that this team keeps its Kanban board while the digital team works in sprints, that is tailoring (tailor to suit the project).

teach.text: Classic traps: the project manager does not 'make sure user requirements are met'; that is the chief product owner. Agile does not remove business justification; it tailors it (project canvas, MVP). Iterations are not management stages. Tailoring changes how principles are applied, never which principles apply.

items: Match the action's purpose to the principle, then check the reason explains this case.
Manage by exception: tolerance on what is delivered, zero on time and cost; the key to self-management.
Learn from experience: short feedback loops, customer involvement, inspect and adapt, retrospectives.
Focus on products: prioritized, decomposed product descriptions flex what is delivered.

summary: You can now identify which PRINCE2 principle an action in an agile scenario applies, using the agile application of each principle in Table 5.1. You can also reject options whose principle is right but whose reason, or role, does not fit the case.

A.q: Saltmarsh Housing Group's service design team holds a retrospective at the end of every two-week iteration. It also tries each new contact-centre script with five tenants before rolling it out, and changes the script based on what they say. Which principle is MOST clearly being applied?
A.why: Many agile concepts support learning from experience, such as shortening the feedback loop to the customer, continual customer involvement, inspect and adapt, and retrospectives (Table 5.1).

whyNot.0: Focus on products is about defining outputs and their quality, not learning loops.
whyNot.1: Tailoring is about adapting the method to the project, not gathering feedback.
whyNot.2: Manage by stages is about the board authorizing one stage at a time.

A.q: Saltmarsh's board sets zero tolerance for time and cost on every level of plan, but lets the number of new features in each release vary. The project manager will raise an exception only if the Must have features are forecast to miss. Which principle is being applied?
A.why: Manage by exception sets tolerances and delegates within them; in agile it allows tolerance on what is delivered and restricts it on time and cost (5.2.1.5, Table 5.1).

whyNot.1: Manage by stages is about authorizing one stage at a time.
whyNot.2: Justification asks whether the project is still worthwhile, not how authority is delegated.
whyNot.3: Focus on products is about defined outputs, not setting tolerances.

A.q: In starting up Repairs Reimagined, the project manager proposes Deborah Kiely, who works closely with the tenants' panel, as chief product owner, and Raj Malhotra as product owner for the service design team. Each person agrees their role description. Which principle is being applied, and why?
options: Tailor to suit the project, because roles must be renamed for agile
Focus on products, because each role owns a set of products
Define roles, responsibilities and relationships, with the right people
Manage by exception, because each role carries its own tolerances
A.why: This principle puts the right people into clear roles and engages stakeholders; in agile, extra roles may be needed and PRINCE2 roles tailored carefully (5.2.1.3, Table 5.1).

whyNot.0: Roles are adapted for agile, but the action is about getting the right people into clear roles.
whyNot.1: Owning products is not why these people were chosen.
whyNot.3: Tolerances are delegated to some roles, but the action here is assigning people to roles.

B.q: Before any work starts on Release 2's parts list for engineers, Saltmarsh's team writes a product description with quality criteria and agrees with the contact centre exactly what the list will and will not include. Which principle is MOST clearly applied?
B.why: Focus on products delivers well-defined outputs, preventing unnecessary work and scope creep and setting clear expectations (5.2.1.6).

whyNot.0: Nothing in the stem is about feedback or past lessons.
whyNot.2: The stem defines an output; it does not test whether the project is worthwhile.
whyNot.3: No tolerances or delegation limits are being set.

B.q: Saltmarsh's project manager, Sally Greaves, tells the board she will personally make sure tenants' requirements are met in every release, because she wrote the project brief. How well does this apply the 'define roles, responsibilities and relationships' principle, and why?
options: Well, because the project manager runs the project day to day for the board
Well, because the project manager wrote the project brief
Poorly, because the senior supplier sets the tenants' requirements
Poorly, because the chief product owner ensures user requirements are met
B.why: The chief product owner represents the user community and ensures user requirements are met; the principle is applied poorly if the PM takes that on (5.2.1.3, Table B.1).

whyNot.0: The PM does manage day to day, but that does not make user requirements the PM's responsibility.
whyNot.1: Writing the brief does not move the user-side role to the PM.
whyNot.2: The senior supplier represents those delivering the products, not the users.

B.q: At the end of stage 2, Saltmarsh's board reviews the one-estate pilot and authorizes stage 3 only. It will decide on stage 4 at the next stage boundary. Which principle is being applied?
B.why: A project is planned, monitored and controlled stage by stage; the board authorizes one stage at a time (5.2.1.4).

whyNot.1: No tolerances are discussed; the stem is about authorizing the next stage.
whyNot.2: The decision is about stage authorization, not defining outputs.
whyNot.3: The board is applying the method, not adapting it to the context.

C.q: A Saltmarsh board member proposes dropping the business case for Repairs Reimagined because 'agile projects discover value as they go', and relying on tenants' feedback instead. Is this an appropriate application of 'ensure continued business justification', and why?
options: Yes, because frequent releases bring benefits to tenants earlier
Yes, because the tenants' panel represents users' needs directly
No, because justification must stay valid; a canvas can replace the document
No, because the business case is the project manager's control document
C.why: A project must have valid business justification throughout; agile tailors the business case, for example to a project canvas with value focus and an MVP, rather than dropping it (5.2.1.1, 6.3.2).

whyNot.0: Earlier benefits are an agile strength, but they do not remove the need for justification.
whyNot.1: User input is valuable, but it is not business justification.
whyNot.3: The verdict is right, but the business case is owned on the executive side, not by the PM.

C.q: The service design team is new to iterations and its members' agile maturity varies. Project manager Sally Greaves proposes reporting each person's maturity to the project board as an issue so that the board can deal with it. Is this an appropriate application of 'learn from experience', and why?
options: Yes, because the board must see every issue on a PRINCE2 project
Yes, because each gap in skills should be logged as an issue
No, because agile maturity is first assessed at project closure
No, because varying maturity is handled openly as lessons are learned
C.why: Varying levels of agile maturity are not escalated but handled transparently as lessons are gathered with the team (Table 5.1).

whyNot.0: The board manages by exception; it does not deal with every issue.
whyNot.1: Skill gaps are handled through learning and coaching, not by escalating each one.
whyNot.2: Agile maturity is first assessed in starting up or initiation, not at closure.

C.q: In initiation, Sally Greaves agrees that the service design team will keep its Kanban board and two-week iterations, while the digital team works in sprints. She records these choices, and the workshops to be used, in the PID. Is this an appropriate application of 'tailor to suit the project', and why?
options: Yes, because tailoring chooses frameworks, artifacts and workshops for the PID
Yes, because tailoring makes every team follow the same agile framework
No, because the principles of PRINCE2 cannot be tailored to a project
No, because tailoring decisions are recorded in the project canvas instead
C.why: In agile, tailoring means deciding which frameworks, artifacts and workshops to use and recording this in the PID (5.2.1.7, Table 5.1).

whyNot.1: Tailoring fits each team's context; different teams may use different frameworks.
whyNot.2: The principles are not tailored, but their application is; this is applying the tailoring principle.
whyNot.3: Tailoring is recorded in the PID; the canvas is the business justification.

reteach.title: Purpose first, then the principle
reteach.question: Can you match an agile action to its principle and its real reason?

blocks.body: Still worthwhile (business justification). Learning from feedback (experience). Who does what (roles). One stage at a time (stages). Limits and delegation (exception). Defined outputs (products). Fitting the method to the context (tailor).

head: Action
Principle
rows: Zero time and cost tolerance, flex features
Kanban here, sprints there, in the PID

blocks.text: A true statement is not enough: the reason must explain the action. User requirements are the CPO's job, not the PM's.

explain.body: Justification must stay valid throughout. In agile it is supported by a focus on value, an MVP, the project canvas and frequent releases that bring benefits earlier.

test.q: Saltmarsh's chief executive says a measurable fall in second visits is the minimum improvement that makes Repairs Reimagined worth continuing, and the board checks this at each stage boundary. Which principle is being applied?
test.why: A project must have valid business justification throughout its life; checking the minimum worthwhile improvement does this (5.2.1.1).

whyNot.0: No roles are being assigned; the stem is about whether the project remains worthwhile.
whyNot.1: No lessons or feedback loops are described.
whyNot.3: No tolerances are delegated; the board is checking value.

explain.body: Tolerances let the board delegate and still stay in control. In agile, tolerance is allowed on what is delivered and restricted on time and cost, which frees teams to self-manage.

test.q: Saltmarsh's digital team decides for itself which Could have portal features to drop when an iteration runs short, and tells the PM only if the release's Must haves are at risk. Which principle does this BEST show?
test.why: Manage by exception is at the heart of empowering people to self-manage within tolerances, flexing what is delivered (Table 5.1).

whyNot.0: Nothing here concerns authorizing a stage.
whyNot.2: The team is acting within limits, not drawing on lessons.
whyNot.3: No roles are being defined or assigned.

explain.body: Get the right people into clear roles and engage stakeholders. Additional agile roles may be needed and PRINCE2 roles tailored carefully. The chief product owner makes sure user requirements are met.

test.q: Saltmarsh appoints a chief product owner to represent tenants across both teams, adding a role that its earlier projects never had. Which principle does adding this role apply?
options: Tailor to suit the project, adapting the method to the context
Focus on products, defining the outputs each team will deliver
Define roles, responsibilities and relationships for the users
Ensure continued business justification for the investment
test.why: Under this principle, additional agile roles may be needed and PRINCE2 roles tailored carefully (Table 5.1).

whyNot.0: Tailoring adapts the method overall; adding the right role for clear responsibilities is the roles principle.
whyNot.1: The action is about a role, not a product.
whyNot.3: The action does not test whether the project is worthwhile.

explain.body: Focus on products: define outputs; in agile, product descriptions, quality specifications and tolerances can be prioritized and decomposed to flex what is delivered. Tailor: adapt to size, complexity, risk and context, choosing frameworks, artifacts and workshops, recorded in the PID.

test.q: To meet the needs of tenants whose first language is not English, Saltmarsh adds translated versions of the online repair form to the product description for Release 1. Which principle is being applied?
test.why: Adding defined product versions so the output meets users' needs is focus on products (5.2.1.6).

whyNot.0: Tailoring adapts the method, not the product's content.
whyNot.2: No tolerances or delegation are involved.
whyNot.3: No lessons or feedback are described as the cause.
